❓
Big Question
Today’s Wonder

After two staves, something is already moving in Scrooge. Is it fear, memory, or love doing the work? Build a claim you can prove.

🎯
Objectives
By the end of this lesson…
📖Reading: I will name the figures of speech Dickens uses and what each one adds.
⚖️Argument: I will argue what is changing Scrooge, with evidence and reasoning, and write a theme statement Staves I and II can support.
✏️Grammar: I will check my own writing for comma splices and run-ons.
📝Writing: I will revise Quick Write 1 and turn in Week 1.

The Song of the Shirt
Thomas Hood (1799–1845) · published 1843 · from stanza 4 of 11
0:30 AI voice reading, not a recording of Thomas Hood.
🖍️ HighlighterTap the two lines that say what the men are really wearing out.
· · ·
"Oh, Men, with Sisters dear! Oh, Men, with Mothers and Wives! It is not linen you're wearing out, But human creatures' lives! Stitch—stitch—stitch, In poverty, hunger, and dirt, Sewing at once, with a double thread, A Shroud as well as a Shirt.
· · ·
3“A Shroud as well as a Shirt.” What does Hood mean?

Hood’s theme is a sentence too. Try one: People who buy cheap shirts…

linen: cloth made from flax, used for shirts · human creatures: human beings · double thread: thread doubled for strength · shroud: the cloth a body is wrapped in for burial
Text: Thomas Hood, “The Song of the Shirt,” Punch, Christmas number, 1843, from The Poetical Works of Thomas Hood (Project Gutenberg #15652). Public domain. Picture: Gustave Doré, Ludgate Hill, 1872, a generation after the poem. Public domain.

Step 1 · Figure It Out
1“solitary as an oyster” (Dickens, Stave I)
2“Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire” (Dickens, Stave I)
3“his mind flew back again, like a strong spring released, to its first position” (Dickens, Stave II)
4“The ancient tower of a church, whose gruff old bell was always peeping slily down at Scrooge” (Dickens, Stave I)
5“its overflowings sullenly congealed, and turned to misanthropic ice.” (Dickens, Stave I)
6“where the shadow of the growing tree would fall” (Dickens, Stave II)
7“a spring-time in the haggard winter of his life” (Dickens, Stave II)
Pick one of the seven. What does it make you see or feel about Scrooge that a plain sentence would not?

One · A comma alone cannot join two thoughts
The chain slipped, I gave up.→The chain slipped, and I gave up.
Two · Then is not a joining word
The chain slipped, then I gave up.→The chain slipped, and then I gave up.
Three · A semicolon joins close partners
The chain slipped, I gave up.→The chain slipped; I gave up.
